newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU, U.S. both claim victory in Helms-Burton twist.
newsitem.headline: EU, U.S. both claim victory in Helms-Burton twist.

text.p: The European Commission on Thursday welcomed Washington's decision to excuse an EU company from penalties under the U.S. Helms-Burton Act, saying the move demonstrated how toothless the law was.

Peter Guilford, spokesman for European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan, said the Commission had been assured that Italian telecommunications company Stet International had not broken EU laws in brokering a deal to avoid U.S. anti-Cuba trade legislation.
His comments came after the U.S. state department and Cuban exile groups hailed the deal as proving just how effective the Helms-Burton Act was.
The Stet development is the latest twist in an 18-month row that at one stage seriously threatened transatlantic trade relations.

The U.S. State Department said on Wednesday that Stet had paid America's ITT Corp an undisclosed sum for a free hand in the Cuban telephone system which ITT built and operated until it was seized by communist authorities in 1959.
EU sources told Reuters the sum was around $25 million.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the deal exonerated the Italian company from liability under Helms-Burton over its holding in Cuban telecommunications company ETECSA.

A section of the Helms-Burton law -- an amalgamation of years of American anti-Cuba legislation -- bars senior executives of companies deemed to be "trafficking" in property seized from U.S. nationals in Cuba from the United States.

Burns said the settlement "sends a clear signal to foreign companies in Cuba using confiscated U.S. property that they will either have to reach agreement with U.S. national claimants ... or face visa denial/exclusion sanctions".

The Cuban American National Foundation, an influential emigre group, called the deal a victory but said it still opposed Stet's presence in Cuba, "subsidizing tyranny and profiting from the misery of the Cuban people."

Another section of Helms-Burton allows U.S. nationals to sue foreign firms using their confiscated property in Cuba, but has been waived three times by President Bill Clinton, most recently last week.
The Act's passing in May last year prompted a furious response from the EU, which deemed the laws extra-territorial.
As well as launching a complaint through the World Trade Organisation, the EU also passed blocking laws making it illegal for European companies to comply with any aspect of Helms-Burton.
This compliance includes disinvesting from Cuba as a result of the Act, although the EU law says a waiver would be granted if an affected company's interests in the U.S. would be hurt.
Guilford said the Commission had been aware of the Stet negotiations "for weeks", but another EU official said the deal had been a complete surprise.

"Stet have given us their word that they have operated in conformity with the rules," Guilford said. "It is clear the Americans know Helms-Burton to be unenforceable, toothless, and so it is no suprise they are happy to settle the matter.

"Our policy is to press for democratic change in Cuba by encouragement with trade. The U.S. seeks change by boycott and embargo. It is clear that with this deal Stet will be allowed to continue to operate, and expand, in Cuba so I would say this is firmly in line with European policy."

Although Washington has compiled a blacklist of companies it suspects of investing in Cuban-nationalised U.S. assets, it has only ever publicly named Stet, Mexican company Grupo Domo and Canadian Mining conglomorate Sherritt International as being in violation of Helms-Burton.
